Mr. Speaker, on June 16 I asked the
Prime Minister whether the agreement between England and Russia of July 3, 1922, was endorsed by Canada, and whether the government of Canada had definitely recognized the union of the Soviet Socialist Republics; and, further, whether the government recognized the so-called Ukrainian People's Republic. I put the question because of certain actions now before the courts. It seems to me only reasonable that we should know where we stand in this regard.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I regret having been
absent from the House one or two days last week and thus unable to answer my hon.
friend's question. By minute of council of December 26, 1921, the Canadian government-approved a formula suggested by His Majesty's government to make applicable to Canada the provisions of the trade agreement between His Majesty's government and the Russian Soviet government of the 16th March 1921. Effect was given to this decision by an exchange of notes dated the 3rd July, 1922, between the foreign office and the Russian trade delegation in London, so that the agreement should apply to the Dominion from that date. Canada's formal recognition of the union of Soviet Socialist Republics was conveyed to their offical agent in Canada, Mr. A. Yazikoff, in a letter from the Prime Minister dated the 24th March, 1924. Among the States included in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics which Canada has recognized is a Ukrainian Socialist Soviet Republic. Canada has not, however, recognized the Ukrainian People's Republic.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What is proposed here is simply to add to the existing clause the words:
Or who is guilty of sexual immorality or any other form of vice.
The act as at present framed does not cover such cases, and the judges have asked that these words be added.

On a hasty reading of the amendment, I gather that it virtually constitutes, as respects a juvenile, a new offence. I am not saying that, even if it does so, it is wrong, but the effect of it should be clearly understood. The Criminal Code clearly defines immorality of this character, but heretofore no juvenile guilty of it was a juvenile delinquent within the meaning of the act. If this goes through it virtually makes the judge the arbiter of what constitutes a vice on the part of a juvenile delinquent. This bill will take the matter out of the hands of parliament and the judge will be made the arbiter. Are we not going to get into a condition where we will have a rather variegated system of jurisprudence under which we will have a Nova Scotia magistrate deciding a thing is all right, and a Manitoba magistrate deciding it is all wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
A tribunal for children
must be considered in quite a different light from a tribunal for other persons. It is not proposed to send children to gaol, or anything of that kind. The object is to have young boys and girls under the supervision of probation officers with the object of trying to reform them. A discretion will be given to the magistrates which they did not formerly possess. I do not think the provision is likely to foe abused. In any case, the amendment is in the interest of the children themselves, and for the proper administration of the act.

us a definition of a "juvenile delinquent ' as it has been used in legislation up till now?

words has been suggested not only by the courts, but by all the organizations such as the Rig Sisters and the Big Brothers, and associations for the protection of children, in Toronto, Montreal and all the big cities, especially in western Canada. All the probation officers and juvenile delinquent judges had a conference, I think last year or the year before, and they unanimously asked that this amendment should be made. I am not especially anxious to have the amendment placed in the statute if there is any objection; I am simply proposing to parliament what all those who are interested in child welfare work have asked for.
I am not objecting; I am simply trying to find out what the amendment means. Does my hon. friend say that the term "or other form of vice" will be confined to offences under the Criminal Code?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

I did not think
he would. Then are we not permitting magistrates-some of whom may be and undoubtedly are very estimable men, although they are not all of that class-to assume the functions of parliament and to say that such and such an act is an offence? It may be a good thing to do; it may be a good thing to say that the whole list of actions having regard to children ought to be looked upon as vices. But if we are going to do that we might consider the child himself to some extent, and also the child's parents. I am afraid this might permit a magistrate to take

Juvenile Delinquents Act
a child from its parents under circumstances which the parents themselves might say were perfectly harmless. In other words before the Criminal Code is invoked against, any individual should it not be plain that it is in connection with some offence we already know about, some statutory offence which is already defined, and which will limit the possible intervention of a busybody? If the hon. gentleman would just point out what is meant by these words, we would understand it. What kind of an offence could his own child be arrested for? He cannot tell us. The former limitation was fourteen years, what is the present limitation?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Sixteen years.

Does my hon.
friend not think that it would be a good thing if the children of Ontario should know that they would be treated the same way as the children of Quebec, and vice versa, and that they could be given to understand that they are being looked after by the lawmakers of their country upon some well-recognized principle in regard to the offences with which they may be made accused? Does my hon. friend really realize that what we are doing here is asking each magistrate to define what vice is, and to legislate in effect upon each kind of vice and form of conduct, irrespective of any action of parliament? Suppose for example you have a child who engages in a game on the Lord's day-that game might consist of trundling a hoop. Some magistrate might absolutely conscientiously think that that was a vice, and might consider that the child was breaking a sacred law. Under this section could that child be taken from his parents and treated as a child requiring influences other than his home influence, in fact treated as a juvenile delinquent, while in the very next township you would very likely find a magistrate who would think that childish games on the Sabbath were not a vice and were not heinously illegal? There is also the other rule which might be applied. A magistrate might read this statute and consider himself bound by the old rule of ejus-dem generis, which would confine use of these words to vices of sexual immorality. But if you read it in that way, the previous paragraph is so broad that	I would
have thought that those other words would be sufficient. I want my hon. friend to thoroughly understand my .point before he replies. My suggestion is not that I think these children should not be looked after by the juvenile court; it is not that we
should not do everything we reasonably can do in order to strengthen the hands of those administering justice in the juvenile court; there is no question we ought to do that. But, having regard to the very important question, ought there not to be a rule for juvenile offenders and ought there not to be a law for them? Ought not a child to have just as much protection as an adult before it can be arrested?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: As I stated, this amendment has been suggested by associations for the protection of children. I have one letter from the Toronto League of Women Voters, suggesting the words "or who is guilty of sexual immorality or any other form of vice". I agree with my hon. friend that in ordinary legislation and in ordinary cases it would not be desirable to leave the words "or any other form of vice" in that vague form. But the point must arise that the whole spirit of the act is to protect children, and to give the magistrates who are appointed for the purpose of presiding over these juvenile courts more latitude and larger discretion. It is not designed to do any harm to children or their parents, but to help them. It has been considered, in the experience of those judges who are spending their time in that social work, that the clause as it stands on the statute is not sufficiently broad to give them all the latitude which they require. After discussing the matter with those who are promoting the legislation, and after offering the suggestions which my hon. friend has offered, I thought there were good and sufficient reasons in support of the amendment, and I have taken the responsibility of presenting this bill to the House. But I did not originate the clause myself.

What is the right of appeal?
I think there should be a right of appeal. I imagine in the main the clause would work out all right. I can conceive of cases where perhaps injustice might be done, but so long as protection by way of appeal is afforded, I would be disposed to support this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see any right of appeal in the Juvenile Court Act.

I am inclined to agree with the criticism of the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton). I can quite understand the desire of certain people and certain organizations to strengthen the legislation in this respect, and if I were certain that magistrates would always exercise a wise discretion I think I would have no objection
Juvenile Delinquents Act

to this provision. But it seems to me to give too much latitude to the magistrate as the provision stands at present. For instance, a young boy of fifteen years might be caught smoking cigarettes, and some person whose sensibilities would be outraged by such conduct might lodge a complaint. That boy might be brought before the magistrate; the magistrate might be of the same turn of mind as the complainant, and the boy consequently would become a juvenile delinquent. I am not overstating the case when I give that as an illustration. I do not know that it is wise to clothe magistrates with that extensive power. As it stands it would incorporate a rather dangerous principle into our criminal procedure.

I think I would be disposed to go as far in this direction as any hon. member of the House, as long as I felt that our footsteps were safe. I have the greatest sympathy with the organizations which have been conferring with the Minister of Justice, and I can realize their difficulties. I presume they encounter cases of depravity that do not come within the provisions of the code, and that cannot very well be brought within the terms of the code, as the code necessarily is applicable to all people old and young. The law as it stood up to the present time has been in brief this: That wherever an offence against the law is charged, we have never yet gone so far as to say to the magistrate :>
In the case of people below a certain age you shall be the judge of what is right or what is wrong; although this child may have offended against nothing within the purview of the code or a by-law or an act of a legislature, still if you think the child is committing what is not morally in its interest, we leave it to you to take care of it under the Juvenile Delinquents Act. That is very dangerous.

Is the age not fourteen
instead of sixteen?

The minister says sixteen. I would go this far, because I am disposed to go just as far as we safely can,-include the words "who is guilty of sexual immorality," but I would not like to allow any magistrate to define in his own mind what an offence is.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
accept the suggestion of my hon. .friend and to amend the section as suggested. I move that the words, "or any other form of vice" be struck out.

Section as amended agreed to.

On section 2-Release on probation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is to authorize the court to adjourn from time to time the disposition of the case as well as the hearing. As the old section stood, the hearing could be adjourned; but when all the witnesses had been heard the judge had to dispose of the case immediately, although it might have been better that sentence should be suspended or judgment deferred and the boy or girl placed under the supervision of some probation officer or in charge of some good people. There is nothing contentious about this.
The second change in the section is that the fine which the court may impose is increased from ten dollars to twenty-five dollars. The judge, of course, still has discretion in regard to the amount, and he may impose a fine of one dollar if he thinks proper.
The last change is to give authority to the judge to impose such further or other conditions as may be deemed advisable. This was not in the original act. One condition, for instance, may be when the case is one of theft that the deliquent should make restitution of the money.

If that is the
only matter that is sought to be covered, it is not necessary at all. As a matter of ordinary practice, my hon. friend well knows, a judge has often adjourned sentence in order to see whether restitution will take place or not. I know we always did that in the old days.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
But no harm will be
done by having that inserted. It may be for other purposes too, conditions in a general way. I am simply quoting this.

It cannot be
for that. It must be for something else. Is it intended that further and other punishment may be inflicted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

The word "condition" I suppose, has to do with the child's conduct. One condition you put on a man or on a child is restraint. Does this mean that there is the possibility of other penalties being inflicted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No. I do not think
my hon. friend is doing justice to those who are asking for these amendments. They are not trying to punish the children; they want

4 p.m. friend seems to think there is something mysterious about the whole matter and that they want to punish somebody. If that were the spirit of the amendments, my hon. friend would be right; but it is not. I do not think there is anything very dangerous in this.

I do not know
that there is. I am trying simply to find out what the minister really wants done.

speechtext:
I will give my hon.
friend the reasons that have been given to me by those who are really promoting this bill:
The fourth amendment proposed to subsection one of section sixteen by adding the words " and may impose upon the delinquent such further or other conditions as may be deemed advisable," is again for the purpose of giving the court wider discretion in dealing with children for their betterment. The right to impose conditions as, for instance, the making of restitution-
I was not so far astray.
.	.	. .etc., has been questioned and while such a
right probably exists-
As my hon. friend rightly says:
-under the present act yet it is better to make the matter clear by the suggested amendment.

Why is it deemed necessary to increase the maximum fine from ten dollars to twenty-five dollars? What little experience I have had has been that the parent always has to pay the fine and very often a parent who can least afford to pay it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The judge of the Juvenile Court at Regina, who is secretary of the association, has written us as follows:
In the western provinces where people are isolated, many of them living on farms removed a considerable distance from town or city, when a boy is proved to be a juvenile delinquent, it is impossible -to place him properly on probation, for the simple reason that there is no probation officer near him to whom he can report. Many of the delinquents belong to the new Canadian type, and to simply return them to their parents when they are not sent to an industrial school, with merely a warning and no probation and no fine, means, that they do not realize they have committed an offence. The only possible way to touch some of these people is through their pockets. And some of same boys work on farms and in harvest time especially earn large wages, and it was thought that in cases where a boy is earning his own wages a fine of ten dollars was too small. It was for these exceptional cases that the amount was suggested changed to $25.
And further on:
The question was fully discussed, and while -we felt that possibly some of those acting as juvenile
court judges might take advantage of the large fine, j'et we felt on the whole that most of the judges would not.
It is also stated:
The idea of a fine is somewhat foreign to the juvenile court system, where the action taken is always what is best in the interests of the boy; but there are of course exceptional cases where it is desirable to impose a fine, and the association-
That is, all the judges.
-considers that the limit should be $25 instead of $10 as at present.
It is suggested especially to cover western cases.

I think that when a fine is
imposed on a boy under sixteen years of age it simply means a fine upon his parents.

The punishment of the
parent through payment of the fine, although sometimes undeserved, is indirectly the best punishment that can be imposed for the offence. A fine of twenty-five dollars for some parents might be less felt than a fine of ten cents in other families. I think I can see a fair reason for increasing the fine to the limit. It does not necessarily follow that the magistrates will impose the maximum.
Section 2 agreed to.

This imposes a responsibility
upon the municipality. Personally I would not be in favour of this clause unless there is some very distinct provision in the bill defining what shall constitute a resident of a municipality.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have myself had experience to which my hon. friend refers. In the province of Quebec when the government is claiming from a municipality the cost for hospital patients there is sometimes much difficulty in deciding which municipality is responsible. But in this case we are doing something for the advantage of the municipality, because the clause in the original act reads as follows:
In every such case it shall be within the power of the court to make an order upon the parent or parents of the child or upon the municipality to which it belongs to contribute to its support such sum as the court may determine.
When the means of the parents are not known, the order has always been against the

municipality. This amendment is to give the municipality the right to reclaim the money from the parents, a right which the original clause did not give.

I do not think
that settles the point raised as to whether the child belongs to a certain municipality. In other cases it has been found necessary to define residence as meaning, say, one year's residence in the municipality. The act says simply "the municipality to which the child belongs." Does one day's residence give a municipality a claim upon the child?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The ordinary law of
domicile and residence does apply.

It would, of course, where
there is no definition of what constitutes residence, but in some acts and regulations there are definitions.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There must be some
rule of practice in Ontario as to that; the courts must decide what length of residence is considered necessary in the case my hon. friend referred to. The same jurisprudence would apply there.

As a matter of fact regulations have been passed for dealing with the question; where there is no regulation, one can become a "resident" of any place the very moment of setting foot there. That of course, is another feature. I must admit that when I first looked at this section I did not quite appreciate its significance, but we have often to look at these things in a great hurry. I see that all this section does is to give the municipality the right to recover from the parent or parents any money paid by it in the first instance. Cases might arise where there are no parents but only guardians. What about such a case? And, further, what about a Barnardo boy?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

On section 5-Adults liable who contribute to delinquency.

What is the
reason for the change, and what does the change involve?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will give the reasons
as they have been communicated to me by the association:
Section 29 making adults liable for causing delinquency in children is a most useful section but one sometimes difficult to work under. It is the view of the association that if a parent or guardian neglects to prevent a child's becoming a juvenile delinquent that should be an offence and that proof should not be made more difficult by the retaining of the word " wilfully."
The proposal to insert the words "or are likely to render " in the ninth line of the section is with the object of making more certain and effective the amendment to -the same section contained in section 3 of the amending act of 1921 11-12 George V, chapter 37. This amendment was adopted in view of certain decisions in western courts which rendered the section practically nugatory.
It is to punish those adults or guardians who act in such a way as to render children

Juvenile Delinquents Act
juvenile delinquents even though the children do not actually become juvenile delinquents. The word "wilfully" is omitted to compel those who are Charged with proceeding in such a way as to make their children juvenile delinquents to prove that they should not be punished.

I would direct
attention to the distinction between a mere act of omission which the conditions might make excusable, and an act of commission. This provision would seem to place in the same position the Fagin who teaches children to steal or makes finished criminals of them, and the unfortunate man who is not able to give his children proper support, proper care, or proper teaching.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would not go as far
as that. The other offence my hon. friend refers to is punishable too.

Yes, by a fine
not exceeding $500 or imprisonment for a period not exceeding two years. That is not a sufficient punishment for a person who turns out children as thieves or who is trafficking in their bodies; the punishment there is entirely out of proportion to the seriousness of the offence. It is certainly very much worse to behave that way with children than it is with adults, yet there would be a far heavier punishment under the Criminal Code for such an offence in the case of an adult.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This legislation will not do away with the penalty imposed by the Criminal Code against the parent or guardian if what he does is criminal. Surely he can be convicted under the ordinary law.

I do not know.
I am inclined to think that where you have a provision dealing with crime generally and ihen a subdivision dealing with juvenile delinquents, and when in addition to dealing with the juvenile delinquent himself you further deal with the abettor or creator of the juvenile offender, if you like, then you are creating a particular offence. We are here creating an offence which has particular regard to the juvenile delinquent, but we go further and we say to the person who has had an active hand in making the child a thief or directing him into immoral practices:	"You are a
person who not only wilfully encouraged but aided and abetted and connived at the commission by this child of an offence under the Criminal Code"

for we say that a juvenile
delinquent is any child who violates the provisions of the Criminal Code. Let us at least know what we are doing here. We are treating in the same way the person who is actively engaged in the promotion of criminal acts of the vilest character against children and against society, and the person who, perhaps through ignorance, perhaps through poverty, neglects to do something which ought to be done for the child. Does my hon. friend not think that this section ought to be broken up with a view to our taking some cognizance of that distinction? Should we not have a very heavy penalty for the Fagin, and deal gently with those who are doing perhaps the best they can but who by mere neglect place themselves, under this provision, in the same category with those who commit the criminal acts to which I have referred?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We are not doing what
my hon. friend suggests; we are not changing the law with regard to such criminals as he has described. They have been subject to the penalty inflicted by this act, and they will still be subject to it. My hon. friend seems to think that the penalty should be increased I do not know that we should go further than the people who are interested in this work are asking us to do. It has not been suggested by anybody that those who are acting in a more nefarious way than others should not be more heavily penalized, all that the amendment purports to do is to make it easier to obtain a conviction under the circumstances, by not making it necessary to prove that, the conditions complained of actually rendered the child a delinquent, nor that there was wilful neglect-the mere fact that the conditions exist, renders them subject to the penalty, unless they prove that they are not responsible for those conditions.

The minister says that the
design of the amendment is to make proof easier, and that the penalty is not being increased.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the same.

quite unintentionally, are misleading in this case. They are supposed to cover the amendments as well as the words which are underlined, but the minister will see, if he looks at the very last of the section, that the penalty is increased to two years, whereas in the original act it is only one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There was an amendment to the act in 1921, and I think the penalty was then increased to two years.
Juvenile Delinquents Act

I would not
blame the minister at all for increasing the penalty; I think some of our penalties are entirely inadequate. I think, for example, the penalties for indecent assaults are inadequate-only two years, for a crime which you could not fittingly describe. But what I resent is to put in the same category with an unspeakable villain like that some poor unfortunate who has not been able to give his children the benefit of better conditions. I do not think the real criminals get enough, and I really fail to see why a person should be charged with neglect which he knows nothing about, and be put in exactly the same class we were discussing a moment ago, for that is the effect of taking out the word "wilfully". 1 do not think that is proper legislation. I want to make it easy to look after the children, but in doing that we ought to have proper penalties for those who offend against the statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be
sure that his remarks will be drawn to the attention of those who are interested in this work, and will be considered by the department also. The main reason why there was so much objection to clause 4 from Toronto and Montreal was that it had not been approved by the association, and that is why I have moved that the clause should be stricken out. I find that my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) is right. The penalty was one year even after the amendment of 1921, and obviously that is being increased to two years.

Does the minister think that
it should be increased? Of course, there might be cases where two years would not be enough, but in the main one year is a severe penalty, and when you consider that a fine of S500 may also be imposed, together with one year's imprisonment, I should think that ought to be sufficient; especially in view of the further fact, which is a fact so far as I know, that there is no appeal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
West York (Sir Henry Drayton) seems to think the penalty too lenient. My hon. friend knows that the magistrate has discretion. It is not exceeding two years, but it may be only one month, it may be fifteen days.

I do not know what the minister's experience is, but I have had a good deal of experience in matters of that kind, and it is astonishing how many of the magistrates seem to think that if they divide the limit in two it is about all right. I do not say they always do it, but there is a tendency to compromise always, and if the fine is $50 they are apt to strike it at $25, and if it is $20 at $10. Apparently the minister did not intend to make the penalty two years. There was evidently no intention to change the law in that respect, which provided a penalty of only one year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no objection to leaving it at one year.

The explanatory note
says the word "wilfully" is strick out before the word "neglects" in the seventh line, but there is no word "neglects" in the seventh line.

speechtext: I noticed that myself. It is a mistake. I think it is in the twelfth line.

Not in this subsection.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I myself would not go as far as that. It would all depend on the circumstances, which will always be known to the local man who will be in charge of the administration of this act. I agree, it is

We can say offhand that we are endeavouring to legislate against such neglect that a magistrate might say was a neglect; I do mot think that, from our present discussion, we would go any further than that. Are we really leaving the definition of "neglect" in the hands of the bench, o.r are we dealing with "neglects" which cou'ld properly be looked upon as connected with some criminal matter or likely to bring about some criminal affair? Going a little bit further, I come back to my former query: Is the neglect legislated against here a. neglect to furnish the child with such necessaries and the like as would prevent its being a dependent, neglected child under the Ontario Act or any other similar act? I think they go a little bit further than we do-is it to be confined to a neglect to give instruction to a Child as to the meaning of a crime, or is it a neglect to move a child from conditions which might suggest crime to it? speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
All the things my hon.
friend has described would influence a judge in giving his decision.
But the magistrate will not be legislating. We are.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The conditions my hon.
friend has mentioned may be such as to justify a judge in convicting a man, but they may not warrant the sending of the mam to prison or fining him severely. The words in the bill
"or are likely to render a child a juvenile delinquent"' should have been underlined, because they are additions, and also the word "two" in the last line.

As to the question asked
by the hon. member (Sir Henry Drayton) I am inclined to think the danger he fears would be remote and that the parent would not be punished unless he was, by his own action, directly aiding the child to become a delinquent. However, I think we can easily imagine a class of cases where the parent would be an agent in the commission of offences by the child as the latter left the 'home from day to day.	-

I quite agree
with what the hon. gentleman has said; that is how the section ought to be read. perhaps a very ignorant parent to teach a child proper ethics would only indirectly tend to produce the conduct sought to be corrected. Let us take a concrete case; my hon. friend may, perhaps, argue that it is too elemental in character but it will serve to illustrate the principle involved. If the father knew his child was going out stealing pennies, even though he himself did not receive the stolen money, he Should be punished. If he knew the child was committing this offence and did not reprimand him or prevent him, he is guilty.
Sir HENR\ DRAYTON: I quite agree.

But, as to teaching the child and making him to understand the difference between right and wrong, if we went into that matter I think we would be on visionary ground, and the parents should get the benefit of the doubt. The magistrate, of course in such cases, should have common sense to do the right thing. He would have to take into consideration the environments of the boy and the parents. If the father were an illiterate man the magistrate should not deal with him so strictly as in cases where the father was not illiterate.

I would go even further than my hon. friend. He says the magistrate should have common sense to do the right thing. I say we should have common sense to do the right thing here in the first place. I point out also that in the first case referred to, if the parent knows the child has gone out to commit an offence he is accessory before the fact and is already liable.
Yes, if he abets the commission of the crime.

His mere knowledge makes him liable under the Criminal Code. He is liable as an accessory before the fact and subject to the same punishment as the young offender. The duty to stop that sort of thing is cast upon him, as the duty is thrown on every citizen to prevent crime. If a person knows a crime is about to be committed, it is his duty to see that it is prevented. I was pointing out that that cannot be the case here because that is already covered.
I am afraid a great deal of this is already covered by some severe punishment already.
It ought to be.

I agree with my hon.
friend. The danger is that the lesser punishment here might displace the present severer punishment.
My impression is that it is removed by this legislation. I think that is the most dangerous part of this legislation, because I d'o not know whether it can be done under this.

I think, rightly or
wrongly, that this is more or less experimental legislation, and whether we should enact a law of this kind or not I do not know. I am not quite sure that these societies are able to handle the child problem. It is a very difficult matter, and they have not had as much experience perhaps as they will have. Whether it is wise or unwise to pass a law that is more or less experimental I would not take upon myself to decide. Yet that is the position here. We are making this experiment and bringing the child under this law.

I do not object to it being experimental, and I do not object to doing anything I can to advance the interests of the child; but I am objecting to the provision with respect to adult offenders, who, I think, are not severely enough dealt with in this section, and the mixing up of a real adult criminal with an innocent man.

The more I think of this
provision the more I am convinced that the section is going too far, although I am convinced the section is framed with a desire to do what is best for the child. It cannot be argued for a moment that this is anything but a criminal section, because when the punishment to be imposed is one year's imprisonment or a fine of five hundred dollars, or both, it becomes very serious, and surely it is unwise to drop the word "wilful." I quite appreciate the effect of the addition of the words "or are likely to render." But I say do not strike out the word "wilful." Take an illustration:	A parent who would bring
himself within the facts I am going to outline could certainly be convicted under this section. We will assume that curfew rings at eight o'clock, or nine o'clock. Suppose a father permits a boy of fourteen to remain out between nine and ten o'clock and to continue that course of conduct, and that boy commits a theft or some crime which brings him within the interpretation of the section, that boy becomes a juvenile delinquent, and the father could be convicted under this section. But I doubt if the father

Juvenile Delinquents Act
could be convicted if the word "wilful" were there. Surely, before we render a man liable to imprisonment for one year and to a fine of five hundred dollars, he should be guilty of something wilful. It should be proved that there was some animus in his mind, because that is the foundation of all criminal acts. I suggest that we should restore the word "wilful" after the word "child," and eliminate the words "and being able to do so," leaving the other words "or are likely to render." If you are going to make the punishment one year, that punishment should only be imposed in cases of gross neglect. The father might be away, and he might have left instructions that the child should not be permitted out at night. Before the father could be convicted under this provision I think it should be proved that he was a paTty to the offence.

I agree with the remarks
of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. boys). The words "or to remove the conditions which render or are likely to render a child a juvenile delinquent" have been inserted on account of a series of cases in which the father of the family persisted in allowing one member of the family, who was notorious in the community to remain at home. The effect was to corrupt the younger members of the family. The mother may have desired to have one daughter removed from the household, and the father persisted in having her at home, although her society no doubt corrupted the younger female members of the family. No provision then in force, however, could deal with that case. The case was brought up before the Police Constables' convention, or the facts of the case were forwarded to them, in order that some action might be taken to prevent a recurrence of a case of that kind, where there was no provision which would deal effectively with it. This provision may go (further than was perhaps actually intended, but it seems to me to deal with that particular class of case, if it is so interpreted and read by the judicial officer before whom such proceedings might be taken.

I am not familiar with the
case mentioned by the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon), but I would have thought from his recital of the facts that such a parent would come absolutely within the provisions of the former section. Surely, under this section, the parent, knowing that such a state of affairs exists in his house and permitting it to exist, is doing so "wilfully." The strong point that I desire to make is that
a severe penalty is provided here. I am not objecting to it; I am commending the minister and all those behind the provision in their efforts to do what they are seeking to do. My one point is that if we make a man a criminal and put him in prison for a year and fine him five hundred dollars, without any evidence to connect him and to show he is the guilty man, we are going too far. I would not be prepared to pass this section on the suggestion that this is a matter ifor the magistrate to consider. We know there are many magistrates of experience, but there are many magistrates who are not lawyers and who have not had experience. They are tremendously influenced by their surroundings and they become considerably worked up at times. In this way a man might suffer where he never should suffer as a criminal. If the word "wilful" is restored I feel satisfied that any case will be met in which a parent should be subjected to imprisonment for one year,

What could be done in the case of a father where a daughter, say over eighteen years of age, was boarding at home, a member of the family, where no act of immorality was committed in the home, but who was notorious for her immoral conduct, who came home for her meals and lived there and who must necessarily exercise an evil effect upon the younger female members of the family? The former act does not deal with such a case, because there is no act of participation by the head of the household in anything which would tend to the moral delinquency of the child; but under this amendment the section would deal with a case of that kind because the father was failing to remove from the family the source of the influence that tended to cause the delinquency?

That raises in a very neat way the very point that I wanted to raise. If I understand my hon. friend aright, he goes this far: The girl in question is notorious, but apparently her notoriety has not reached the mind of her father. Would it be proper, under those conditions, that the father should come within this section and be imprisoned for a year? The whole thing is one of knowledge. If the father knows that he has such a girl in his household, then he is within this section and his neglect is "wilful". If he does not know this-and that is the case put by my hon. friend-surely he should not be held responsible. A man cannot be guilty of a crime if he is not directly associated with it. In the case cited, I submit with all respect, the father cannot be held to be a criminal.
Juvenile Delinquents Act

In the twelfth line of page 3 of the bill there are these words:
Being the parent or guardian of the child and being able to do so, neglects to do (that which would directly tend to prevent a child's being or becoming a juvenile delinquent.
The expression "being able to do so", having the power, must mean, it seems to me, having the knowledge, because he would not be able to exercise that power unless knowledge was brought home to him.
I agree with my hon. friend that that implies knowledge. That is my exact point. The moment you get knowledge you get wilful conduct. That is why I want to see that inserted in the bill.

While wilful conduct is
implied in this, the actual word "wilful" is not used. But it indicates there is power of suppression of the evil condition that exists, and if he is able to suppress that evil condition and does not do so, my suggestion is that he becomes guilty of an offence under section 4.

I should think the word "wilful" should, in any event, be restored. The question of ability is ambiguous. He might be able if he had the knowledge. "Being able to do so" means, I think on fair reading, that he is in a position of authority to straighten out the regettable state of affairs provided that he knows about it. I would strongly support the idea of removing the ambiguity by restoring the word "wilful".

I have had some cases
under this act. The word "wilful", as my hon. friend knows, has a peculiar signification before a judge. It means a deliberate act, a knowledge brought home in such an emphatic way that there can be no question that the person guilty of the offence had it brought home to him, not in a constructive way, but in a most definite and positive
5 p.m.* way. The defence in many of these cases is that the person did not know. Take the ordinary case of a father who has young children at home, who is guilty of a persistent course of profanity, of assault upon his wife, assault upon the children and generally a course of conduct of that character. That would bring him within this section. But it does not deal with those peculiar cases where the mother, perhaps, wishes to have the home wholesome, but some member of the family, perhaps a sister of the father or some other member, a boarder, is kept there in defiance of the wife's wishes.
With knowledge?
Yes.
Then it is "wilful."

I have had a case in the city of Peterborough, where, in spite of the mother's attendance on the chief of police, the father deliberately persisted in keeping this person in the household, and he had a right to do so.
Will my hon. friend not agree with me that that is really a case of wilful conduct?

I do not think "wilful"
goes that far. "Wilful" is such a deliberate, determined refusal to accept the condition as laid down that it goes far beyond the interpretation which might be constructively put upon knowledge, that is, knowing that a condition exists. Supposing this case existed: Knowledge is brought from the chief of police to the head of the family that a certain member of his family is of the type of character that would cause delinquency of the younger children. After that notice had been given to him, he would be put upon inquiry and would be guilty of an offence under this legislation unless he satisfied himself in every reasonable way that there was no ground for the suspicion that was indicated to him, say, by the chief constable. That would be, perhaps, a wilful breach of this section. I am submitting that to my hon. friend in order to prove that wilfulness must-go far beyond what must be real knowledge brought home by evidence of members of the family who have learned from time to time the evil conduct of this person who has been kept in the family in spite of knowledge being brought home to the head of the household. It might be said that this is not wilful because it was a sin of omission, not of commission; that is there was 'not the positive act, but neglect in permitting the matter to drift. It is just to deal with those cases, it seems to me, that this particular section is worded in this manner.

My hon. friend, I think, is
putting upon the word "wilful" too severe a construction. But, lest he be right and I be wrong, I would suggest to the minister that, instead of the words "being able to do so," he insert the word "knowingly". My whole point is, knowledge; I think it must be shown that the man has knowledge. To convict a man of crime and take any chance of sending him to prison for one year without showing that he has any knowledge of the wrong is abhorrent to me. I do not think

Juvenile Delinquents Act
the word "wilful" is too strong. It was in the act before, but if it is thought that it is too strong, let the wording be as follows: Being the parent or guardian of the child knowingly neglects to do so.

I agree with my hon.
friend (Mr. Boys), and I think as respects almost every crime you could bring forward the same argument about the deletion of the word "wilful" ingeniously used by the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Gordon). Careful as he generally is in language, I agree with the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) that he went too far in his definition of "wilful". The word does not necessarily mean a determined wilfulness; it means a substantial degree of knowledge. You bring home to the accused that with that degree of knowledge he lets this thing go on from day to day. I can see no objection to putting in the word "wilful", for we must assume that the judge or magistrate will at least be of average intelligence and that on the evidence he will be able to decide as a juror the issue of wilfulness.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The word "wilfully", the elimination of which is proposed, was discussed by the association to which I have referred at its last convention. It was then unanimously decided to ask for the elimination of this word because in Rex v Hoffman. 1919, 1 Western Weekly Reports, page 625, and Rex v Limoges, 1921, 1 Western Weekly Reports, wage 293, convictions could not be secured against the offenders because of the word "wilfully" in the section, although in the opinion of all the members present at the convention the conditions justified convictions.
Was there something peculiar in the facts in those cases?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have sent for the law reports. I find that I made a mistake a few minutes ago when I said that two years instead of one was a change; I was right in the first instance when I said that the amendment of 1921 covered it, section 3 of chapter 37, which substituted the word "two" for the word "one". So, as it is now, there is no change in the term of imprisonment.

That only emphasizes my
contention that it makes the offence all the more serious.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is my reason for withdrawing my assent to the change.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the two cases I have
mentioned the word "wilfully" in the section prevented convictions.

That in itself would not perhaps warrant the dropping of the word here I do not argue for one moment that the use of the word "wilful" in statutes does not frequently stand in the way of convictions; I say it does, and I say it should when we are talking of crime. Under the Ontario Temperance Act we find provisions that a man shall be presumed to have knowledge of this, that and the other thing, and he can be convicted of many offences without the Crown actually proving that he had knowledge of any guilty actions. But that is a different state of affairs altogether.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I agree to "knowingly."

I think that would be fair
under the circumstances.

the committee that section 5-now section 4 *-be amended in the thirteenth line by adding after the words " to do so " the word " knowingly."

Do you think
that would work out well?

Putting "knowingly"
before neglects."
It is just merely inserting the word " knowingly " instead of the word " wilfully."

subtopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT, 1913, AMENDMENT

speechtext:
The House resumed from June 20 consideration in committee of Bill No. 176, to amend the Gold and Silver Marking Act, 1913-Hon. Mr. Low, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 2-"Platinum" to be applied only to articles of defined component parts.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. LOW (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: GOLD AND SILVER MARKING ACT, 1913, AMENDMENT
speechtext:
When this matter was previously under consideration I maintained that what the Jewellers' Association had in mind was that the word "platinum" was to be applied to any article of which 95 per cent of the total quantity consisted of platinum. In a report received from Mr. W. J. Ryan, Inspector of the Gold and Silver Marking Act, among other things he states:
At the fifth annual convention of the Canadian Jewellers' Association, which was held at Windsor, February 13, 14 and 15, 1922, and at which over 300 jewellers from all parts of Canada were present, among the business problems discussed was a proposed amendment to The Gold and Silver Marking Act regarding the stamping of platinum goods. At a meeting of the executive committee held on the 5th of December it was decided that application should be made at the next session of parliament for an amendment to The Gold and Silver Marking Act to provide for the marking of platinum articles. The committee recommended that the title of the act be changed to read " The Precious Metals Marking Act, 1924," and that a new section be inserted to cover platinum articles, worded as follows:
" The word ' platinum ' or any contraction, abbreviation or colourable imitation thereof shall not be applied, either alone or in connection with any other word, to any article of merchandise composed wholly 3r in part of any metal unless 950/1000ths of component parts of the metal appearing or purporting to be platinum of which said article consists are either the pure metal and element platinum alone or in conjunction with iridium."

I always thought that the jewellers had in mind that the article should be 95 per cent platinum, but the leader of the opposition in several Statements ridiculed the idea. When the Deputy Minister of Justice came into the House the other day the right hon. gentleman put certain questions, and the deputy agreed with the interpretation placed on it by my right hon. friend. I had not the slightest doubt in my mind at eleven o'clock in the morning that he had told me that it meant 95 per cent of the whole article. But he whispered to me that since I had been in his office he had read the debates of the day before-I did not question him as to whether the opinion of other lawyers had impressed him or caused him to change his mind. He further added that these sections were not drafted with the idea in view that they should be interpreted by the ordinary layman in the House; rather was it intended that the courts should interpret them. I allowed him to go out of the chamber. But the leader of the opposition made this statement:
There can be no possible two opinions on the subject. The opinion is just, what the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice told the minister a while ago, and what we have contended for for two days, I do not think it is the object of either the Jewellers' Association or the framer of the bill that the whole article should be 95 per cent platinum.
And again he said:
The minister is wrong as to his conception of what the draftsman intended. The draftsman who drew this never in the world intended the whole article to be 95 per cent platinum-never.
I had stated in the House that the president
or the secretary of the association had told my deputy over the long distance telephone that what the section meant was 95 per cent of the whole article, but again the right hon. leader of the opposition disagreed with me. I was glad to know that there were a few hon. gentlemen who did agree with me. If hon gentlemen will refer to page 3395 of Hanusard they will find that the hon. member for King*, N.S. (Mr. Robinson) said:
The intention doubtless was that it should be 95 per cent of the element platinum, but it does not say so.
He agreed that that was the intention. Again, on Friday last, the 20th, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) stated:
That is the meaning I put upon this clause. In other words, whatever metal it is composed of, 95 per cent pure platinum or platinum in conjunction with some other metal shall form part of the whole composition.
In order that there might not be any mistake, I telephoned to the secretary of the Jewellers' Association, to satisfy myself that the opinion my deputy had conveyed to me

Gold and Silver Marking
was correct, and the secretary replied: "There is absolutely no doubt that was the intention." I said, "Come down here to Ottawa, so that you may be able to verify it." He said, "I will send the chairman of the association." The chairman of the association came down, and afterwards I addressed the following letter to Mr. John C. Strachan, chairman, Canadian National Jewellers' Association, Toronto District:
I attach hereto a question asked by the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen in the House of Commons on Friday. Will you be good enough to advise me which of the questions he asks is correct? I shall esteem it a favour if you will give me the answer in writing.
And the question I attached to the letter was the very question asked by the right ban. leader of the opposition on Friday last. I did not wish to put it in my own words, because I knew my hon. friend would probably doubt it had been properly put, so I simply attached the following clipping from Hansard:
Mr.. Meighen:	As to the plainness of the clause
it is a matter of opinion. As to the meaning of the clause it is not a matter of opinion, it is very clear, I would not have risen but I see the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice here, and I am going to put the two interpretations in his hearing and ask him to give the opinion of the department as to which it is. The question is this: Whether in the case of an article, a single article, as respects which part purports to be platinum and part not, this bill insists that the whole article shall be 95 per cent platinum or part platinum and part iridium, or whether only the part that purports to be platinum shall be 95 per cent platinum and iridium? I want the assistant deputy minister to answer himself.
The reply I received to that letter was as fallows:
Hon. Thos. A. Low,
Minister of Trade and Commerce,
Ottawa.
Sir,-In reply to the question asked in the House, a copy of which you attached to your letter, I beg to advise you that the intent conveyed in the first question correctly represents the desire of the jewellery trade-i.e. that an article to have applied to it the word-" platinum, or any abbreviation of the word platinum," must contain 95 per cent of the gross weight, or total contents of platinum, or any combination of platinum and iridium.
I have the honour to remain,
Your obedient servant,
John C. Strachan,
Chairman Canadian National Jewellers' Association, Toronto District
That, I think, bears out the statement that I made as to the intention of the jewellers. I also informed the right hon. leader of the opposition, that that was what the president of the Jewellers' Association 'had told me over the long distance telephone, but he doubted me. I perhaps have given the act 223
more attention over the week-end than before, and I have discovered that it contains a clause providing that:
The Governor in Council may, from time to time, make such regulations as to him seem necessary or expedient for declaring articles to be exempt from the application of ithis act.
I am sure that the right hon. leader of the opposition knew of these orders in council that had been passed; he knew a great deal more than I did; he knew that if there was any remedy required in connection with this section it could be provided by order in council. However, in view of the opposition raised by certain members of the House, I desire to withdraw the bill.

speechtext:
So far as I am concerned I do not propose for one moment to be under any such cloud as that. Surely to goodness it is not fair to suggest, when we on this side of the House make suggestions regarding the phraseology of a clause appearing in a bill, that we are objecting to the bill itself. We were, just making some suggestions a few moments ago to the Minister of Justice in connection with a bill he had before the House, and it is only fair to say that he accepted some of those suggestions. The Minister of Trade and Commerce now says definitely, and I think if he is fair he will admit he did not say it quite so definitely a day or so ago, that 95 per cent of the whole article, or as the chairman of the Jewellers' Association perhaps better puts it, 95 per cent of the gross weight, shall be platinum or iridium. Now all we have been endeavouring to do here is to point out to the minister that we want the wording of this section made so definite that a layman can construe it and understand it. It may be that a jeweller or a judge might understand it as it stands, but you want to think of the public who are not experts, too. The very beauty of legislation is that its wording shall be such that any man of reasonable intellect can read it and understand what it means when he reads it. I made a suggestion the other day to the minister, and I am going to make it again before he presses for withdrawal of this bill, because there is not the slightest desire on the part of any one on this side, and I think I can speak for every one, even for my Progressive friends, to interfere with the provisions of this bill in any way. We are simply trying to make the wording definite, and I would ask the minister to consider this suggestion. I would suggest that the section be amended to read as follows:
The word " platinum " or any contraction, abbreviation or colourable imitation thereof shall not be applied, either alone or in combination with any other

Gold and Silver Marking

word, to any article of merchandise composed wholly or in part of any metal unless 95 per cent of component parts of the metal of which the whole of mid article consists are either the pure metal and , slement platinum alone or in conjunction with iridium.
I think this does exactly what the minister says he wants. Surely the minister will be fair, and when at least eight or ten members of this House, all acting in good faith, express a doubt as to the meaning of the section, he will admit that there is some doubt. I am certain that he has the desire to have this section made definite, and now that we know that the 95 per cent applies to the gross weight, if the language I have suggested, or some similar wording of which the English language is certainly capable, is used, there can be no further doubt. I would ask the minister to consider that suggestion before he presses for the withdrawal of this bill.

speechtext:
As far as I am concerned, I make no request at all; the minister can withdraw his bill or not, just as he likes. All I am concerned with is that he is not going to put me in any false position. I made a certain contention as to what the bill meant in its present form, namely, that the exaction, of the bill applied only'to the portion of the article which purported to be or was apparently platinum. The minister disputed it. I asked the minister to get the opinion of the justice department. He called the Assistant Deputy Minister of Justice in and he agreed distinctly with me after the minister had told the House that the Justice department were all against it. Not only did he agree, but virtually everybody in the" House agreed with the contention. Yet the minister persisted and persisted. Now he makes his appeal from the Justice department as to the effect of the clause to the Jewellers' Association. Well, I decline to submit myself to the jurisdiction of the Jewellers' Association. The Jewellers' Association may be a very fine institution, but it never was created for the purpose of determining the meaning of a legal statute. It may have been their intention that the whole article should be 95 per cent platinum or platinum and iridium, I do not know as to that, but the Jewellers' Association is not a court of appeal as to the meaning of a statute. Nor did I express any opinion as to what the chairman of the Jewellers' Association would say. I am ready to submit to the opinion of the Justice department, but after this in the case of the minister I would rather somebody else would endeavour to carry that opinion to the House than he. I endeavoured to adhere to
the opinion not only of the Justice department but of the Law Clerk of the House.
The bill was referred to the Department of Justice and Mr. Newcombe wrote as follows with respect to it. The letter is dated 12th January, 1924:
Referring to your letter of the 24th ultimo, asking that a draft bill to amend the Gold and Silver Marking Act, 1913, be prepared by this department for your minister's consideration, I have the honour to enclose same herewith.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,

But my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, and other members of the House, insisted that the section was, to say the least, very clumsily framed. On many occasions during the last few days you will find the clause characterized by the right lion, gentleman in that way. Now, an hon. gentleman, who is a lawyer I know, gets up here and suggests that the amendment be drafted1 in a certain way. Is it possible that one hon. member of this House can, in a few minutes, draft a better section than the Department of Justice was able to do in two or three months.

If the minister will permit
me I will convince him that the suggestion made was not unusual or unreasonable. Not thirty minutes ago, when we were considering Bill No. 116, to amend the Exchequer Court Act, introduced by the Minister of Justice, a suggestion was made-as the minister says here more or less hurriedly-but it appealed1 to the Minister of Justice. He accepted it, struck out certain words, and amended the section. Are we to understand that if a bill is brought forward, even if it has passed through the hands of the Deputy Minister of Justice, that we are debarred from criticising it or from offering any suggestion for its improvement? That is practically the attitude of the minister. As far as I am concerned these suggestions are made in good faith. I want to see the bill go through in the interests of the public as well as in the interests of the Jewellers'

Gold and Silver Marking
Association. It is most important that the word " platinum " or the word " sterling " or the words " solid gold " and! so on should not appear upon articles of jewellery unless they contain exactly what they are supposed to contain. Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 190, to amend the Canadian National Railways Act, 1919.

C.N.R. Act Amendment
This item was not induded in the business mentioned on Friday night. I do not know whether we ought to press the objection or not. What is the bill?

My right hon. friend will
remember that last year the Guarantee Act of the Canadian National Railways, was amended in the Senate in reference to the guarantee of the equipment bonds. The amendment to the bill raised the question whether it did not take away altogether the right of guarantee equipment issues, the Justice department was consulted, and they thought it did.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
On section 1-Guarantee only on authorized issues.

The hon. member for
West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and myself have discussed this matter a good deal. The other day I read the brief that counsel for the Canadian National Railways had put into my hands, as follows:
Paragraph 4 of section 2, of this last-mentioned bill reads as follows: "Nothing herein contained shall be construed as granting power to guarantee any securities the issue of which has not been authorized by parliament."
The trouble with this paragraph 4 was that it prevented, in the opinion of the Department of Justice, the issue of equipment securities for the reason that equipment securities are obligations of the Canadian National Rolling Stock Company, Limited, which is a company incorporated under the Dominion Joint Stock Companies Act. General power is given the Dominion Joint Stock Company to issue securities, but the Justice department considered that paragraph 4, as above quoted, was dealing with specific authority to issue a specific amount of securities and that the general power in the general act to issue securities did not comply with the wording of the paragraph. Consequently we propose to amend the paragraph to read this way:
" Nothing herein contained shall be taken to authorize the guarantee of any securities the issue of which has not been authorized by this act or some other act of parliament."
The " some other act of parliament " covers the provisions of the Companies Act, and we have added the words "this act" so as to overcome the objection which was raised, but not seriously pressed, that the provisions of paragraph 4 destroy the power to issue securities given to the company by the Canadian National Railways Act itself.
For the purpose of further restricting the company in its issue of equipment securities, I have added the
second clause to the draft bill to the effect that where parliament has authorized expenditure on equipment to the extent of 25 per cent of the cost, the company may make, or cause to be made, one or more equipment issues for the remaining seventy-five per cent of such cost; that means that in order to make equipment issues in the future we will have to go to parliament and obtain an appropriation of the 25 per cent down payment, which is always made in cash. When this appropriation is passed no further legislative authority is necessary to enable us to issue securities and, if deemed desirable, to have them guaranteed for the remaining seventy-five per cent.
That is, that the. requirement of the act that parliamentary authority must be obtained will be complied with when parliament passes an appropriation for twenty-five per cent of the proposed issue.

When the bill was up
before, the minister stated that the government was ready to engage itself not to guarantee securities under the act of last year or under this amendment except to the extent that the amount was included in the estimates of the year. I hope I have not misunderstood the minister on that?

That does not include
equipment issues. They are made on what is called the Philadelphia plan under which 25 per cent cash is paid and 75 per cent is issued as securities, the roiling stock purchased being the security for the 75 per cent. But these issues never go in the estimates., What I said the other night, and what I think my right hon. friend is referring to, is that we have no idea of departing from the practice of putting regular railway issues in the estimates.

That is to say, for all
other purposes except equipment-
Yes.

[DOT]-the amount shall be in the estimates. I may say that equipment security guarantees have not been in the estimates before, for the simple reason that there were none. I think the minister will search in vain for any.
There were last year.
Yes, $22,500,000, but tlx re were none by the, previous government. My opinion is that they ought' all to appear in the estimates. If we adopt this practice it will be very hard to get away from it.

Bonds are issued for 75
per cent of the equipment, and under what is known as the Philadelphia plan the amount due is amortized and so much paid every year
C.N.R. Act Amendment

into a sinking fund to repay the bonds at the end of a certain term. I do not think you will find that they were ever placed in the estimates. Of course, branch lines are dealt with in separate legislation.

They never were in the
estimates because there were no equipment guarantees until last year.
Yes.

No. Mr. Fielding the
year before advanced about a million and a half dollars for equipment purchases, and the previous year we advanced about fourteen million dollars odd. This money of course was in the estimates, but at no time until this past year was any guarantee given of equipment securities. I do not say there were not equipment securities isisued, but they rested on their own feet. I am not objecting to the principle of guaranteeing equipment securities, but I am not convinced that there is any real difference merely because a different system of payment is adopted. Every security issued has got to be paid. The equipment issue is given special security on the equipment, and I know other issues give a special security of their own, The equipment security provides for yearly payment; other securities do not, they provide for payment at maturity. But what difference that makes on the principle of including our liabilities in the estimates I am not able to see. My contention is that until the hour comes when the National Railway securities that we are responsible for are themselves assets to us equal to their face value, the amount of our responsibility we ought to always include in the estimates, and include in our debts our liabilities as respects the road. If we do not do that we may just as well take all our other securities which already have been added to our national debt, and which no longer are regarded as active assets, and regard them as active and deduct them from our debt. In a word, we have no right to say to the people of Canada that our responsibilities are such and such until the asset we take for our responsibility is equal to the amount of our liability. Consequently, it seems to me, the minister would be well advised to put all these things into hhe same catalogue exactly and include them in the estimates, and in our debt, until he is able to recover from the company interest on the mortgages we hold.

Unlike the loans to the
Canadian National Railways, the government is asked to contribute nothing directly to this particular loan except the 25 per cent
[Mr. Graham.1
that it pays in cash, and the securities for the balance of 75 per cent are issued against the new rolling stock purchased. As I said before, a certain amount has to be paid annually over a term of years until the whole is amortized. Now, putting it in the estimates would of course imply that the government must guarantee, otherwise there would be no necessity for it being placed there.

But it is just the same
as any other estimate, if the government does not guarantee it the expenditure is that much less.

But my hon. friend from
West York- (Sir Henry Drayton) and I the other night when discussing this matter agreed that it is well to have in the act a power to guarantee.
I think so.

As far as the New York
market is concerned, the government guarantee practically amounts to nothing, the United States understanding so well the system under which these securities are issued, but in Canada it does make a perceptible difference.

As a matter of fact, does
not the government guarantee the other 75 per cent?

This is authority to do
so.
What has been the practice in the past? Did the government guarantee the issue last year?
Yes.

Does the government say
that these equipment issues of the National Railway would sell on the New York market at equally as good a price if the government did not guarantee them?
On the New York market I would say yes; but not on the Canadian market.

The minister says
there is a great difference because there is provision for annual payment of these equipment securities. Suppose the Canadian National Railways issued a mortgage for $12,000,000, and instead of making the mortgage bonds repayable in twenty years, with interest at 5 per cent yearly, they made them repayable so much every year, or provided a

C.N.R. Act Amendment
sinking fund for the purpose, would the minister consider that a sufficient reason for not including in the estimates for that year the guarantee of these bonds by the country?

I should not like to give an opinion offhand, but as a matter of fact these equipment issues are under a different system and a different principle altogether from other securities. They are an obligation of the Rolling Stock Company. The Rolling Stock Company primarily has its charter under the Companies Act, and that is one of the reasons for one of the changes in this act. These securities are treated in a separate and distinct manner altogether different from the guarantees of the Canadian National Railways themselves, and they are looked upon with such favour in the United States that a government guarantee is not considered to be of any assistance at all in marketing them. It did not enter my head that it would be necessary to put equipment issues in the estimates.
I do not think the former government guaranteed any equipment issues.
I do not know.

I do not think I am wrong in my recollection. We used to get just as good prices for those issues on the New York market as was got in any other way, and I think my hon. friend is quite right when he says that in the New York market a government guarantee is not of any practical use. Since then a new situation has arisen in Canada in connection with the growth of our war financing; to-day we can raise large amounts of money without guarantee. There is a marked difference between a security issued on rolling stock and any other security. A security issued on rolling stock is one that can be readily realized upon, one of the very few things that a creditor can take in connection with the operation of a railway under the trust deeds. In connection with an ordinary guarantee or ordinary security, summary proceeding is out of the question; receivership is all that can be got. With regard to the amortization, I presume these are ten year bonds?
I assume they would be ten, yes.

My recollection is ten; sometimes they are seven. Ten is about the longest that should be considered. The theory is that as you pay 25 per cent cash and as each year you have to pay a
certain amount into sinking fund, there is not much risk. That is the plan the Americans have worked upon in connection with practically all their loans, and practically without loss. Loss on an equipment issue is a very rare thing; I do not offhand remember any. Frankly I do not think we are in very much danger of losing anything over and above the 25 per cent. But there is a great deal more to this bill than that. When the matter was being discussed the other day I pointed out that under the general act of the 'Canadian National Railways, which defines their present bonding powers, the right was given to the system to issue bonds to the extent of $75,000 per mile, and that I had been told by one of the railway officials that practically the whole.. of that privilege of issuing bonds had been exhausted. In connection with these regular bonds, which are the major part of the bonds of the system-the equipment bonds are very small compared to the regular bonded obligations of the system, -there is a very sharp difference between the position we took in the past and the position of the hon. gentleman. Our position always was that the practice we initiated was right, namely, to include in the annual vote the amount of money required to help the railway out, whether in connection with guarantees or in connection with the furnishing of cash. We drew no distinction between guarantees and cash, and under the legislation of this very year my hon. friend availed himself of the practice that we had followed. Take, for example, his guarantee of equipment securities; he made that guarantee last year under the authority of the vote of last year. At least, that is as I understand it; if my hon. friend has any other legislation I wish he would tell us about it. However, I do not think he has. Now, I was not quite sure that the officials of the road were right about the limit of $75,000 per mile being nearly exhausted, and I put a question on the order paper, the answer to which I received to-day. The answer shows the outstanding funded debt of the Canadian National Railways, exclusive of the Canadian government railways, to be $856,147,056. The owned mileage, which is the mileage on which the right to borrow money would be calculated, is given at $15,668.41. The average per mile of bonds is given at $88,775.41. If these figures were correct I would have no objection to this legislation, because the government would have to come down and get parliament's authority before they could give these guarantees; there would be no right on the part of the company to issue bonds. As the right to guarantee is limited by the right to
