issue bonds, if the right was exhausted then we should be squabbling over something which is not at all material. _ But my hon. friend's officials do not figure in such a way as to show that, or if they do they figure in such a way as to make for their argument and not for the facts. The average per mile of bonds I have given as 888,775. If you divide the amount of owned road mileage, 15.668.41, into the amount of the outstanding funded debt, it is obvious that that gives the amount of bonds per mile. If hon. gentlemen will take the trouble to check these two figures they will find that the amount issued is under

I did not quite follow
that.

There are two questions involved. First there is the matter of the guarantee of equipment securities. In that connection the House is to be informed, because under my hon. friend's own proposal 25 per cent of the whole cost is to be voted in cash.
That is on equipment.

On equipment. So we there do get some control of the system ; we do get these figures submitted to us; we have the opportunity of check and we have the duty of voting. Then, the next proposition is to get an untrammelled right of guarantee. That general right of guarantee, in its turn, is held down by the 875,000 per mile. The figures submitted would show that it had been altogether exceeded, but that figure of $88,000 odd is incorrect. The correct amount is, as I have stated, 855,000 odd per mile. So the effect of this legislation is to give the government the right to issue these guarantees without the considered consent of parliament to the extent of 820,000 per mile ' on a mileage of 15,668. It does not require a very close figuring to show the tremendous extent of the blank cheque which this legislation would entail. If my hon. friend is well advised he will go back to the old practice so far as these votes are concerned. He did it last year and it did not hurt him at all. He is getting the advantage now in connection with his guarantees of 25 per cent. If he would just take section 2 of his bill and drop section 1 he would then be in a position to 
carry on business as we have always carried on, plus the right of issuing guarantees on securities when there was only 25 per cent voted.

I do not quite follow
my hon. friend when he says it would give us carte blanche to issue securities without the sanction of parliament. But let me refer to the other matter first, for my hon. friend's criticism of the figures needs a little elucidation.
My department errs very often in giving more information than is asked for. In this case we were asked only for the bonded indebtedness, but in addition to that they added an amount of something like five hundred odd million dollars that the railways owed the government for loans from the government, not being bonded indebtedness, and they made the amount of indebtedness per mile 888,000. That was not the question asked. The question was, what was the bonded debt? So, deducting the amount of government loans in cash from the totals given in the statement my hon. friend has in his hand, would leave the amount of fixed debt at $856,147,056; dividing that by the mileage, exclusive of the government railways, on which there is no bonded indebtedness-on the Central Vermont there is something like $40,000 per mile indebtedness-would leave $55,000 per mile as the bonded indebtedness That does not include the loans in cash from the government to the railway, these having no bearing on the question of indebtedness It will be remembered that last year Mr. Fielding introduced a bill taking power to grant certain securities. That bill was amended in a way that the Department of Justice informs us possibly takes away all the powers of bonding from the Canadian National Railways, so far as equipment is concerned anyway, and it is rather to restore that power, without depriving parliament of any rights that were purported to be guarded in the bill of last year, that we are introducing this legislation
This bill is amending subsection 4 of section 2 of the Canadian National Railways Guarantee Act, 1923, and that subsection reads;
Nothing herein contained shall be construed as granting power to guarantee any securities the issue of which has not been authorized by bond.
The amendment proposed is this, and I shall submit it to the committee after the explanation I have made:
1. Subsection four of section two of The Canadian National Railways Guarantee Act, 1923, is hereby repealed, and the following enacted in lieu thereof:-

C.N.R. Act Amendment
"(4) Nothing herein contained shall be taken to authorize the guarantee of any securities the issue of which has not been authorized by this act or some other act of parliament."
Some other act of parliament, I presume, refers to-

The general
bill of 1919.

Or the powers of the
rolling stock companies.

The company
has the right with respect to rolling stock.
I do not understand that this gives us carte blanche to authorize guarantees without coming to parliament.

I think it does, and I think I can carry the judgment of my hon. friend. In the first instance, I will come back just for a minute to the question of the guarantee clause my hon. friend has referred to. They are two distinct matters entirely. In so far as the guarantee is concerned, I have pointed out that in that connection parliament's advice is taken, and a vote of 25 per cent' of the guarantee has to be passed. That guarantee, I do not think, is subject to very much risk at all. It is something which has not been found necessary to use in the past. It was used once this year under the regular form \Vhich we have used for many years, under which railway assistance, whether by way of direct grant, guarantee, or anything else, has been given in a supply bill. Now my hon. friend's government, last year came to the conclusion that they did not want to bring down in a supply bill any question of guarantees. We thought they were wrong at the time we took our stand.

That was on the branch
lines bill?

No, on this very issue. Last year we passed a law, which deals in the first instance with the securities of the company. Perhaps I had better read it all:	'
No securities, as defined in this section including in such definition equipment certificates or obligations in any form intended to be issued to the public, shall be issued for the purposes of or by the company or any of the companies designated in the schedule hereto except those approved as to form, terms and amount by the Governor in Council.
I may pause there simply to say that there was no objection to that at all. As a matter of fact, there was no need for it, because'the company always had to come to parliament, and we had complete control over
it, but there was no harm in taking further control, and so there was no objection. The next clause reads:
The said securities so approved may be guaranteed by His Majesty and any such guarantee may be in such form and on such terms and conditions as the Governor in Council may determine, and may be signed by the Minister or Acting Minister of Finance on behalf of His Majesty.
The effect of that legislation was to give the government the right to guarantee, without coming back to parliament at all, any securities of which they approved and which were issued by any of these companies. That was the thing we objected to. We said, "You should incorporate this in the supply bill, come back to the House, and in the usual way get your right of guarantee." But the government did not agree with us at all. The matter was taken up in the Senate, and the Senate and government have agreed to this clause:
Nothing herein contained shall be construed as granting power to guarantee any securities the issue of which has not been authorized by parliament.
One would naturally think it would be imprudent indeed for any government to want to do anything more than that. The form is not the form in which we thought it should be in at all. We thought we should still have our supply bill, we should still have our vote, and that parliament should still know exactly where the railways were to be, and what the country's commitments were. That was our position and, speaking frankly, I do not think the amendment in the Senate was a proper or a sufficient one. However, it was something that pleased the government and they took it gladly.
I did not.

Well, my hon. friend perhaps was not here but no objection was raised by the government at all; they accepted it immediately. The difficulty the government find themselves in is this: In consequence of the opinion given by, I think, the law officers of the government-this is their considered view after this question had been taken up by the legal gentlemen that look after these issues-the construction was put upon this section that the power to guarantee securities is one limited not to the case of the general right of issue but to the specific right of issue. I think my hon. friend will agree with everything I have said so far. That is where the whole difficulty is-that although it may have been thought that this would give a blank cheque, a blank authorization, the lawyers have since held that there being a term of limitation on the powers of guarantee, the

specific right of issuance must be first shown before there is the right of guarantee. I think in this I still carry the judgment of my hon. friend. Finally there is a letter from the Canadian Authors' Association expressing their appreciation of the work of the staff. I should like to say that while these letters convey a well deserved tribute of appreciation to Mr. Tolmie and Mr. McKinnon, the man who more than any other is responsible for the scenic effects and transparencies is Mr. Turcotte, who has been for many years attached to the Canadian Exhibition staff.

I have been from the
beginning very strongly in favour of Canada taking part in the exhibition and also of her part being such that it would properly reflect the importance of the Dominion and the Empire, and I see no reason to criticise the success with which Canada's work has been done. I have not, of course, been able to visit it, but such reports as I have had, let me frankly say, reflect credit on the Dominion. I do not oppose any vote that is essential to the complete success of the undertaking, As respects the feature of the vote which covers a proposed official representation there by members of both Houses and the press, I take a different view from that of the government but not in any truculent way. I think the government would be well advised to withdraw that feature of their proposal. The Prime Minister has referred to a pre-ced<ent when we sent to Chicago an official representation of two. He has referred, as well, to a representation! of much larger 2244
dimensions that went to attend the Coronation of King Edward, and a similar representation that attended the coronation of the present king. These, if I understood him correctly, were all parliamentary representations.
I distinguish between functions of that kind and an exhibition-this exhibition, the Chicago exhibition, or any of a similar kind. The coronation of His Majesty was an event in a category by itself. The reason we were properly represented in such a fashion was to attest the fealty of the Dominion to the person of His Majesty. I think considerable reflection might have been made on Canada, and justly so, had we not sent such a representation of the parliament of Canada as attested the fealty of parliament to his person and his throne.
Of course the Chicago exhibition is a case in point. We were represented there. I would have no objection to similar representation here. In fact, I think it is quite right that a member of the government should be there, so that at functions he may speak as representing the Dominion, and I have not the least doubt that as soon as parliament prorogues, which will be as soon as anyone else can readily go, a member of the government-probably more than one-will go over and represent this country. But that is different from sending a delegation of from eight to twelve members of parliament to the exhibition in any special capacity. To do so would not in my judgment strengthen the confidence of the electors and taxpayers in the country in the good faith and fidelity of their representatives in this House. It seems to me that all that is requisite, in so far as parliament and the government are concerned, is representation which should fittingly be by a member of the government itself. There will be members of parliament there; doubtless many contemplate going. It is to be hoped that they do go, but I do not think there should be a group of others placed in any special position and sent at the expense of the treasury. That is the view I have held and the view I will have to support, and in all earnestness I suggest to the government that they themselves withdraw from the vote such amount as covers what they have in mind with reference to an extended parliamentary representation.

I wish to associate
myself with those who have opposed the principle of this vote of probably 120,000, to send a delegation of parliamentarians overseas. I believe it is true that the whips have

May I ask whether the hon. member has read the official letters

which have gone out from several leading citizens of Canada in reference to the unemployment which they face at the present time? *I refer particularly to Toronto and Winnipeg.

No, I have not read
the articles which the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg refers to; but I will tell him what I think is another of the causes of so much unemployment. Many of those who employ these men cannot get them to earn the money they are asking. A lady keeping a boarding house told me not a month ago that she called a plumber in. He was not in the house more than fifteen minutes; he did not put any new material on the job, yet he charged her eight dollars. That is a sample of some of your unemployed men. They cannot get steady employment and they do not deserve it.

Perhaps he was a
lawyer, not a plumber.

He may have been a
political agitator too. If the whips go over to the Old Country they can honestly make representations to thousands' of people who will be glad to come to Canada and who will, in that way, improve their material conditions very much. With all the hardships we have in Canada-and I admit there are many

conditions are much better here than in the Old Land. We want 'to give those people an opportunity to come to Canada, and while I am well aware that a small percentage that come will not make good, I believe the great majority will make good. This country needs hundreds of thousands, aye, millions of men who are not afraid of hard work. We want men who will work more and talk less than some people we have in this country. I am going to vote for sending those delegates because I think this will be a good investment for the country and we shall get our money back a hundred fold.

As I am more or less associated with this vote I think I should not remain in my seat without saying a word or two. If there is one thing I regret, it is that if the invitation were extended to me as a whip to go over to England, for certain reasons that I need not trouble the committee with, I would not be able to go. I would, nevertheless, appreciate the opportunity of going and enjoying the honour of representing Canada at that exhibition. When one reflects that Canada has invested a million dollars in this proposition and when we are told that other colonies in the Empire are sending delegates, it would be somewhat extraordinary if the largest and most important colony in the Empire had no delegation there
whatever. I may be under a misapprehension as to the number that are going, but what information I have indicates that six are going, four from this House and possibly two from the Senate. I will support the appropriation heartily, and I regret that circumstances beyond my control will prevent my going if the invitation should ever come to me as whip of the party, because I would enjoy that very decided distinction on the part of my country.

The discussion has
wandered entirely out of its proper channels. The discussion was on the question of immigration, and I am not convinced that this has anything to do with immigration at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the British Empire Exhibition.

The Prime Minister
(Mr. Mackenzie King) cleared up at least one point, namely, that the visit was purely a social one. It is based entirely on tradition and precedent, and I would understand, when we are compared with the other colonies that this is just a matter of keeping up with the Jones's. If it were of particular interest as regards immigration, I would say that it would probably be right and proper to take a certain amount of the Immigration estimates for this purpose. I am not convinced of that however; I think our friends who propose to go over to England are going just to have a good time and, perhaps, incidentally to represent Canada. As to how they are going to represent Canada and what particular good they are going to do, I am just a little at sea. I tried to secure from the minister some time ago statements regarding the number of Canadian employees already in England, connected with the various departments, Immigration, Trade and Commerce, and the number of special men they propose to send over in connection with the exhibition. I did not secure that information and I would be obliged if the minister could give it to the committee now.

I have not lost confidence in our fellow Canadians nor in our fellow members of parliament. Whatever action a member of parliament would take on behalf of Canada at the British Empire Exhibition would be creditable to himself and to Canada. I cannot support for several reasons the amendment that has been moved. In the first place, no concrete reason that I can support has been given and) I cannot follow the line of reasoning of those who support the amendment. In debating the amend-
Supply-Immigration

ment they referred to the duties of different members going to the exhibition in connection with immigration. There are more factors in building up Canada than immigration and people do not come out from the Old Country only for the purpose of engaging in farming. I look on this vote for the British Empire Exhibition and upon the money that would be spent for individuals who might go to the exhibition as money well spent. We living in British Columbia are interested in other questions than that of immigrants coming here for the purpose of farming. The people of British Columbia, particularly the fruit growers, have gone to a great deal of expense, time and trouble to send exhibits to this exhibition. The fruit growers of British Columbia have prepared one of the most wonderful exhibits of fruit at that exhibition that any one would want to see. This is the advice that has come to me directly from those who are at the exhibition at the present time.
In British Columbia they have also preprepared a wonderful exhibit of minerals, and I hope hon. members on this side of the House will sometimes take into consideration that in Canada- there are other factors than farming. I appreciate the position they take on behalf of farming and their farmer friends, but I feel that sometimes they lose sight of the fact that in Canada we have many conditions outside of farming, although I will admit that it is one of our greatest assets. We all want to promote in Canada every asset we have and in British Columbia two of our greatest are minerals and fruit growing. At this exhibition, they have done themselves proud in preparing these exhibits with the co-operation of the provincial and Dominion governments. I feel that the procedure taken by the present government in departing from the custom that has been followed in the past is a good one, by appointing certain representative members of the House of Commons, members of the Senate and members of the press gallery so that when they visit this exhibition they will be able to interchange views and accomplish a great deal of good in that way.
In British Columbia we have many undeveloped mineral resources, and at the present time every effort is being made to endeavour to get our Old Country friends to invest money in our mineral resources. With the mineral display on exhibition in England *nd with the different representatives visiting the exhibition on behalf of Canada, I believe a great deal will be accomplished

towards promoting an interest in Canada's natural resources. For these reasons I cannot support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland).

Can the minister give
an answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) as to the number of employees from the various departments? Also, can he give the number of the provincial representatives whose expenses are being paid by the Dominion?

I have already stated-I do
not think my hon. friend was in the House at the time-that we told the provinces they might send official representatives and deduct the expenses from their contributions to the federal treasury on account of the exhibition

That is practically the
same thing. But could the minister answer the other question put to him by the member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) ?
My recollection is that that question was placed on the order paper some days ago. It has to go through the Secretary of State, and I do not carry the information in my head.
How many members do the government suggest should be sent, and from what groups will they be selected?
I stated a few minutes ago that the number would not exceed seven, including representatives from the Senate. The different groups in the House will be represented.

Mr. Chairman, I
hope that the item before the committee will satisfy the people of this country, and I think the government would have been recreant in their duty had they not seen that Canada was well represented at the Wembley exhibition. I do not know of any better opportunity to advertise Canada than this exhibition presents, and I am glad to know that the Canadian building is a very creditable contribution.
But I am sorry that I cannot commend the other feature. I have no doubt whatever that many members of this House will visit the exhibition during the summer, and I do not think it is fair to those who go over at their own expense that they should find there a more distinguished band of fellow members, as impliedly they could be placed in an inferior position by not having been included in this band of official representatives of the Commons. This, I think, is possibly the most objectionable part of the proposal. I thought

Supply-Immigration
that when a few years ago we abolished titles we had become very democratic indeed, but I am afraid that a distinction will be drawn between those members who go over at their own expense and those who attend nominally as the representatives of parliament-a distinction that is not at all desirable. The members of this House who belong to the British Empire Parliamentary League will meet with a very cordial reception from the other members of the league in London, but I have been picturing in my mind the position in which our members will be placed who are not nominated as the representatives of parliament to attend the exhibition. The Prime Minister has intimated that a good deal will be expected of these official representatives on their arrival in England. Well, it may be so. But I have no doubt that the government will follow their usual practice and that most of them will visit the Old Country immediately after prorogation. They are the people whom we expect to represent Canada rather than the parliamentary delegates. Personally I do not see the slightest reason for a selection of this kind, for it will discriminate very severely against those members who visit the exhibition at their own expense. At this particular time it is not wise for us to encourage any expenditures that can possibly be avoided, and I think it is the duty of this government, perhaps as it never was the duty of a government before, to practise the most rigid economy. I objected the other night to an "exhibit" being sent over there-one of the most widely known men in the Dominion-but my hon. friends at the other end of the chamber took exception to my motion to reduce the item by $4,000. I might refer to some other "exhibits" sent over to Great Britain. Certainly I would be sorry to think that our whips, genial, affable and well-liked by everybody in this House, should go across as "exhibits," considering some of the "exhibits" we have already sent across and whose expenses we are still paying. I would hesitate to vote against any item for this exhibition, but I am absolutely opposed to a grant for the purpose of sending over selected members of this House on the mission stated. Many people in this country are to-day bringing pressure to bear on the government on the plea that they are not receiving a living wage-I do not know whether they are right or not.-but when they learn that members of the House of Commons are being sent over on an expedition of this kind at the country's expense, I do not think it is likely to increase their respect for our system of government. If the government wish to send a parliamentary delegation, why do they not introduce in the estimates a separate item for the purpose and accept responsibility for it?

I have not had the advantage of hearing all the discussion, but I have been apprised of the purpose for which the vote is proposed. I think in order to consider the matter in its proper perspective we must first of all realize that we stand here as the trustees, the custodians of the monies raised from the people of Canada, monies raised for the purposes of national government, and I think it is highly improper, indeed highly immoral, for parliament to use money so entrusted to its care for the purpose of spending it in the manner indicated. Consequently I oppose the expenditure as a matter of principle. In these latter days we hear a good deal about the "honour and dignity" of parliament. I am quite satisfied that we are not enhancing either the honour or the dignity of parliament by using these trust funds to give a pleasant month or so to a few members of this House, however desirable that may be to them personally. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I have no hesitation whatever in saying that I believe parliament would be recreant to its trust should it for a single moment countenance this expenditure.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened to practically all the debate on this item, but I am not sure yet just what is the necessity for sending the proposed delegation to the Wembley exhibition, and I think the government is making a mistake in bringing the proposal forward. I understood from the speech of the Prime Minister that he thought we should reward the whips by giving them this trip. While I feel the House is often indebted to the whips, yet I think the proper way for the House to reward their services, if some reward is to be given them, would be to increase their salaries. The people of Canada-that is, those of them who give any thought to this matter-will say that this House is spending money in an improper manner in sending certain of its members on this enjoyable trip. I would like the minister to state to the committee a definite amount that will not be exceeded should these delegates be sent to England. Then, how will members who do not belong to some of the parties mentioned by the minister have a chance of being represented? I take it from the speech of the hon. member for Weybum (Mr. Morrison) that these members are being sent over as immigration agents. When he said we needed millions of men brought into this country I could not help thinking how inadequate this estimate was, when we know that from a grant of $200,000 made to the Canada Colonization Association we secured the large number of 35 settlers.

I have not the corrected answer.
It is on Hansard.
It has been suggested by some hon. member that the press men are to have a representative sent ovpr. Is that correct?
Yes.
Can the minister justify the sending of a representative of the press gallery to this exhibition at the expense of the people?

Yes, I surely can. I should think there would be no cheaper method of getting advertisements for our country than through the press; in fact, it is almost the only way you can get it. The press helped to make my hon. friend; surely he does not object to the press doing a little advertising for Canada?
No, but I expect the minister to give us some better justification than that for spending the money of the people to send a representative of the press gallery to the exhibition at Wembley.
We expect to get returns for our investment.

The minister has not yet answered the question, put on several occasions, as to how many groups in this House were going to be represented-how many from the Liberal party, how many from the Conservative party, how many from the Progressive party-and whether labour was to be represented.

I will be frank with my hon. friend. We started out on the assumption that there were three recognized groups in this House. I think the representatives will be decided on the same basis as that on which the committees of the House are decided.
There are four groups.
Is the Labour group not recognized in this House or in this country?

Yes, there is no objection to recognizing the Labour group, but if we follow the rule that prevails in the appointment of committees I am not sure that the members of the Labour group are sufficient to bring them in under the quota.
Then are the labouring classes of this country not to have a representative from this House?

I did not say so. I said that the Labour group were not sufficient in numbers to enable them to be included in the quota on the basis of the nomination of committees. There is no reason why they should not be recognized.
What is the quota?
My hon. friend can figure that out for himself. He knows the basis on which the committees are appointed.

Seeing that the Labour
group has been brought so prominently into this discussion, let me say this: I understaand that the grant under consideration is to go toward sending the whips of parliament over to the Wembley exhibition. As the Labour whip I want to say right now that I will not go, because I am opposed to the principle. of taking a trip like that at the expense of the public.

I do not want to give
a silent vote on this proposal. I am opposed to sending whips or any other body of members of this House to this exhibition at the expense of the country. This is a year in which I think we can hardly justify any expenditure for that purpose. One has only to look at the estimates, at pages 60 and 61, to see how necessary it is that we conserve our resources. We have found it necessary this year to reduce our annual vote to the Canadian National Institute for the Blind from $20,000 to $10,000. If we must reduce that vote for the blind I certainly would not feel justified in voting $5,000, $10,000 or $15,000 for this little trip. I find on the same page that we have had to reduce our vote this year in the interests of economy from $20,000 to $15,000 as a grant to the Canadian Tuberculosis Association. If we have to pare down that vote by $5,000 this year in the interests of economy, I would not feel justified in spending $5,000 for the expenses of this trip. So with the vote on page 60, Canadian National Safety League, a vote the application of which is familiar to every member of the House. That is reduced this year from $25,000 to $10,000 in the interests of economy. With such a statement as that in the estimates laid before parliament by the government, I think the government should reconsider this matter and follow the suggestion of my right hon. friend and leader that the proposal be withdrawn.

Mr. Chairman, I rise for

I do not want to be discourteous to my hon. friend. He comes from Alberta. We had a conference last fall attended by representatives of all the different provinces. Alberta was represented by Mr. Hoadley, the Minister of Agriculture in the Alberta government, and Mr. Hoadley was most insistent upon it that we should get more immigrants, particularly for his province. I would like to satisfy my hon. friend, but I am bound to say I do not think he represents the views of the people of Alberta. I believe the people of Alberta desire more immigrants, more people to go on the land. The people of Saskatchewan desire more; the people of Ontario and Quebec desire a prosperous Canada. We are not among those who are afraid that our country will be filled up with thrifty and industrious people.

I hope the minister does not insinuate that I am afraid of filling up this country with industrious people. But we have been endeavouring by this policy to fill it up for a number of years and we have not filled it up yet. The United States is often referred to as an example, but I am told that the United States has never spent one dollar for the purpose of bringing immigrants into that country. What the United States did was to make the condiitions in that country such that people were anxious to go there.

Supply-Immigration
By a high tariff?

This immigration policy as at present carried out in Canada is class legislation. If we are to have immigration why should we have it limited to one class? Surely the farmers of Canada are producing enough now. I have been told by a gentleman from British Columbia that they are producing more fruit in that province than they can sell. I have seen potatoes left in the ground because of a lack of market for them.
I have seen cattle sold for one half what it cost to raise them, because there was not a market in Canada for them. There is no question that a great deal of agricultural produce is turned out in Canada which cannot be sold at the cost of production because there is not a sufficient market. Why should we go on trying to get more farmers into Canada? If all other classes of people in Canada had done their share as well as the farmers, there would be no lack of prosperity in this country. To answer what the minister has said about my representing the people of Alberta, I do not pretend to represent the people of Alberta. But I do pretend to represent the people of my constituency, and I say without hesitation that the majority of them would tell the minister just as frankly as I have done that his immigration policy is a class policy; that it is directed against one class. I have resolutions here from farmers' organizations in my constituency protesting against the government spending any more money on immigration until the financial condition of the farmer is made easier and until conditions generally are such that the farmer can make a decent living as well as the other people in this country.

None of us on this side want to stop voluntary immigration. What we are against, though-and we think a good deal more attention should be given to it-is any condition which results in a great number of people leaving this country. We consider that people who have been in Canada anywhere from ten to twenty-five or thirty years are far more valuable to the country than any people brought in with no experience. I wonder if the minister is aware that in spending $3,500,000 last year to bring people into this country Canada lost the entire number she brought in and 45,000 besides? That is why we are anxious to see a change made in the government's policy. It is not because we do not want people in this country: what we want to stop is the exodus of people from this country.

It is true that people were leaving the countiy, and they will do it again next year or any other year if similar conditions prevail: a man who can get $15 a day or $1.50 an hour in New York is not going to work in Canada for $5 a day. My hon. friend would not do it. But the tide is turning the other way: the records show that in the last two months, 9,815 Canadians returned. These are the reports from ten ports.

I object to the implication of the minister's remarks that hon. gentlemen in this section of the House are opposing immigration. If I understand the situation rightly, no hon. gentleman in this section of the House is opposed to immigration. What we are trying to point out is the absurdity of taking people in who have no money and no means of being placed on the land. If the government are determined to carry out a policy of immigration and to bring in some good, hardy, vigorous types of settlers they must at the same time provide some financial means for settling those people upon the land. I came originally from Prince Edward Island. There was a time in the history of that province when they were faced with an almost complete breakdown of agriculture. The difficulty was solved by the provincial government of that day financing the farmers of the whole province-and in this I believe they were assisted in some of the borrowing arrangements by the Imperial authorities-through a system of rural credit which enabled the farmers to buy their own land under long term loans at a low rate of interest. That resulted in resurrecting agriculture throughout the whole of Prince Edward Island, and I understand that the provincial government lost not one dollar. That is one of the things the government must face to-day; if they are prepared to carry out an immigration policy it must be coincident with some means of putting the people on the land and enabling them to remain there. The assumption seems to be that when a remark is made from this part of the House with regard to immigration we are saj'ing something derogatory to the country, something defamatory of the country. But I think a search of the pages of Hansard during the last three years will show that not one single remark in any way reflecting upon western Canada came from this part of the House. The very fact that we are in the country shows that we have confidence in it; the very fact that we are here in this House shows that we have confidence in it and that the people have confidence in us. We have a country second

Supply-Immigration

to none in the world. In the district in which I live we are growing fruit which cannot be equalled in most parts of Ontario. On the farm on which I live wild grapes are growing, all kinds of wild fruit-we can produce almost anything. Gentlemen to our right and hon. gentlemen on the other side refer to us as wheat miners, and all that kind of thing, but the day will come when some of those hon. gentlemen will be down on their knees praying to heaven that we be wheat miners again. What is happening your farmer to-day? Trainloads of our western butter are coming to the East and swamping your markets. Last year seven or eight carloads of dressed poultry came to this part of the country from the West and were marketed in Montreal. What did that do to the eastern farmer? It cut his price just in half.
They are not grumbling.

Thirty or forty years
ago the eastern farmer was almost put out of business when the prairies were opened up and they commenced to grow wheat and oats out there. I have heard the old people talk about it; I have heard them talk about it in the Maritime provinces, and those who lived through that period will remember it as long as they live. They finally got into mixed fanning, and they have now weathered the gale and re-established themselves. We are going through that period in western Canada to-day. We have a hardy, vigorous, virile type of people, and they still have a low standard of living, no matter what nationality they are. They work long hours, and deny themselves a good many of the things that you think are necessary in eastern Canada, and they are producing beyond the limit of this country to absorb. Now, what is the government doing? Last year our exports of butter to England dropped from about 17,000,000 pounds the previous year to 4,000,000 pounds. We have a host of trade agents on the other side trying to get us business, but. they are failing because we are losing that business to New Zealand, Denmark, Holland, Argentina, and other countries. I am quite convinced that if the government would put a little bit of energy behind an effort to go after that trade, they would secure it. I made a suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture when his estimates were before the House, and I give him credit for admitting it, but he stated that the people of eastern Canada were not prepared to submit to the regulations that were necessary to bring our butter up to the same grade as New Zealand butter in the Old Country market. The consequence is that we are losing the English butter market to-day.

Is the advertising which the
minister is doing at these exhibitions in the United States responsible for this flow of ex-Canadians from the United States back to Canada?
That is a method of advertising. It is not a new policy; it has been going on for years.

Of the 9,807 ex-Canadians repatriated, are there any who have not found employment in Canada in the last few months?

Supply-Immigration
I have no complaints before me.

I notice that when people are going over to the United States they are asked whether they are going to stay or whether they are just going for a holiday, and if they say for a holiday, they are allowed tc go through and no record is kept; but when people come back from the United States, whether they have made their home there or are just returning from a holiday, they have to fill out a form, and thus a record is kept and filed in the immigration office of the flow back to Canada. Does the minister think Canada can possibly keep a real check on her citizens who are leaving, when no record is kept of those who are crossing into the United States just for a holiday?

I do not think we can. I do
not think that is kept in any country, except through ocean ports.

Is it not quite possible
we have been losing a great many more people than we have a record of? I know of a certainty of a number of families who have gone over to the United States intending to stay there, but who have said they were just going for a holiday, and if that is the case with others, we may be losing many thousands more than we have a record of.

I asked the minister a short time ago in regard to the amount spent in the United States, and I did so for this reason:	Although the money is spent
for exhibitions the main object is really to promote business and emigration from the United States to Canada. There was spent in the last four years $1,830,669.32 to promote emigration from the United States to Canada.

What was the amount for
each year?

For 1920-1921, $456,870.41; 1921-1922, $419,946.02; 1922-1923, $525,363.90; and from April 1, 1923, to January 1, 1924, $428,488.99. What I am pointing out is this:	In view of the amount which has been
spent over there we have not really been getting value if the tide of immigration is from this country to the United States. Possibly this may have been the effect of the money that has been spent, and I presume the same condition existed before this four-year period* ended. In view of all that is taking place between our neighbours to the south and ourselves, it appears to me that this money could be spent to much better advantage in the Old Land, where we could get a much better class of citizens who would 225i
come out here and likely make homes in this country. I do not agree with those who say we do not need' people in this country to help develop our latent resources. This country was never so much in need of willing workers as it is at this hour, and any one who desires employment in this country can get it at short notice. In the case of those who have not found employment, it is largely because they cannot obtain a certain kind of work they desire. If they were as handy at adapting themselves to conditions in this country as the people of twenty-five or thirty years ago you would not hear much about unemployement in Canada. For that reason I have no sympathy with those who would put up the bars and exclude from Canada those who would make desirable settlers. We have in the Dominion a tremendous undeveloped area, and it is quite evident that our people, or at least many of them, are not inclined to indulge in the manual labour necessary to develop the resources which that area contains. That is the reason I would urge upon the minister to consider the wisdom of curtailing expenses in the country to the south.
